title: Life keeps running out
hookLine: a dewdrop at sunrise, a stream that never stops; and a psalm next door that counts the days too
tomorrow: what if the time runs out before you've even started?

lines: THE ONE NUMBER NO SCREEN SHOWS.
cards: How fast is a life running out? A phone shows screen time to the minute. A watch counts steps and heartbeats.
Nothing on any screen shows the one number that matters. An old teacher in the suttas answered with pictures instead of numbers: a dewdrop on a blade of grass, gone when the sun comes up.

teach.b: In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha tells of a teacher from long ago called Araka, who taught his students with images. Human life is like a dewdrop on the tip of a grass blade, gone at sunrise.
Like a bubble raised by rain on water, gone in a moment. Like a line drawn on water with a stick, closing as it's drawn.
Like a mountain stream, carrying everything along, never stopping for a moment. Then the Buddha adds that life now is shorter still than in Araka's day.
The stream is the picture for today: not a sudden drop, a steady flow. Life doesn't run out at the end. It keeps running out, every breath.
Here's a neighbor who says something close.

teach.h: TEACH US TO NUMBER OUR DAYS.
teach.b: In the Bible, a psalm that Jews and Christians both pray asks, in the King James words: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."
Count the days, to grow wise. Araka would recognize that. Both look straight at time running out, and both say the looking makes a person wiser, not sadder.
And one honest difference. The psalm is a prayer: the psalmist asks God to teach him, and his hope rests in God.
The Buddhist reflection asks no one; it's a training of the mind, and it points toward letting go and toward nibbana. Two neighbors, one shared window, looking out from different houses.

how: Buddhist teachers use images like Araka's dewdrop and stream in talks on impermanence; Jews and Christians pray Psalm 90, and its line about numbering our days is often read at funerals and at the turn of a year.

games.q: what does “life keeps running out” mean?
o: running out of energy at the end of a long day
life running out steadily, breath by breath
a life that has lost its purpose or meaning

games.q: Araka's pictures, and a neighbor's — tap the pairs.
p: gone when the sun comes up
teach us to number our days

s: Buddhism and the psalm say exactly the same thing about time
both say looking at time makes a person wiser; the psalm asks God to teach it, the Buddhist reflection asks no one.
Araka compared life to a mountain stream that never stops
not a sudden drop, a steady flow: life keeps running out.
life only really runs out at the very end
the stream picture says it runs out steadily, every breath.

games.q: your grandmother, a Christian, sends a card with 'teach us to number our days.' your Buddhist friend asks if it's the same as Araka's stream. what's fair to say?
o: it's the same teaching in different words; every tradition says this.
they share a window: count the days to grow wise. the psalm asks God; Araka asks no one.
they're unrelated; one is about God and one is about water.
games.why: shared: looking at time running out makes a person wiser. different: the psalm is a prayer to God; the Buddhist reflection is a training of the mind.

practice: Close your eyes and follow one out-breath all the way to its end, to the small pause before the next one starts. Feel that pause: a tiny ending, and then a breath arriving anyway. Stay with a few of those endings until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Life keeps running out: not all at once at the end, but steadily, like Araka's mountain stream, every breath.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: life, a lifespan; the thing Araka's pictures say is always running out.

carryVoice: One to keep: every breath, a mountain stream that doesn't stop for anyone. Day sixteen thirty, counted.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 7.70 (Araka Sutta; numbered 7.74 in some editions): the dewdrop, bubble, line on water and mountain stream

sources.q: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
